item.title: QE ArXiv Watch: Week of September 07 - September 14, 2026
item.description:
If you’ve ever wished you could design experiments around the decision you actually need to make (not the parameter you happen to estimate), this week’s batch is your jam. Across DOE and reliability, the theme is the same: stop optimizing surrogate metrics and start optimizing the thing you’ll be judged on—policy regret, predictive risk, multi-level guarantees, or “how bad is disagreement really?”

Designing experiments for what we’ll do next (not what we’ll know next)

Two DOE papers basically call out a familiar trap: we run a clean experiment, get tight confidence intervals… and still make a suboptimal decision because we didn’t learn the right thing.

Higbee et al. tackle “second-wave” design when wave 2 exists to support a constrained policy choice. Imagine you already ran a first experiment, and now you get one more shot—but the goal isn’t better parameter MSE, it’s lower Bayes regret under real policy constraints. Their trick is to approximate the welfare surface locally (quadratic near the estimated optimum) and treat the second-wave design as choosing Fisher information. In the Progresa-style subsidy problem, the optimized wave-2 design doesn’t look like “repeat what worked”; it concentrates effort where the marginal welfare gradients live (e.g., more focus on secondary school and high subsidies for a smaller treated group). Reported regret drops are big—often 50–70% versus re-running the original design at the same sample size. For practitioners: this is a blueprint for “adaptive DOE for decisions,” especially when leadership cares about regret not R².

Jakeman et al. push the same idea into Bayesian OED for predictions (QoIs), then add risk preferences in three layers. You can be average-case vs worst-case across QoI components (I-optimal vs G-optimal), and you can also be conservative about rare ugly datasets (not just rare ugly parameters). The punchline is practical: parameter-focused criteria like EIG/KL can be almost indistinguishable from random sensor allocations when the real goal is predictive uncertainty in downstream QoIs. If you’ve ever placed sensors because “information gain said so” and later found prediction performance underwhelming—this explains why.

DOE meets uncertainty geometry: “inconsistency” as a response surface

Mäkelburg et al. reframe consistency checking across interacting CPS models as a response surface: choose an intervention vector θ (changing uncertainty geometry), observe an inconsistency probability I(\theta). They generate datasets with Saltelli sampling and Monte Carlo labeling, then speed everything up with two ideas that feel very QE-friendly:

1) Multi-fidelity Monte Carlo (control variates) that lands nearly on the MC reference at far lower cost (MAE ~0.006-ish versus ~0.05 for crude geometric proxies like AABB).

2) A learned surrogate (a Product-Set Transformer) that predicts inconsistency directly from post-intervention zonotope-set geometry—microsecond inference, i.e., “scan the response surface like it’s cheap.”

Once you can evaluate I(\theta) fast, the fun starts: Sobol sensitivity indices to identify dominant uncertainty drivers (center shift tends to dominate), and “recourse” search (gradient-based or evolutionary) for minimal interventions that restore consistency. In practice, this is a template for turning expensive verification-ish questions into something you can actually explore and optimize.

Reliability: from single guarantees to hierarchies of guarantees, plus better agreement audits

Farzaneh et al. ask a question reliability teams increasingly face: what if one policy must satisfy multiple outage targets simultaneously (think gold/silver/bronze SLAs, or multiple customers with different risk tolerances)? Their RA-DPO formulation maximizes weighted “utility certificates” subject to lower-tail constraints at several reliability levels, and they connect the structure to nested conformal prediction. The bounds are intuitive (a shared policy can’t generally match separately optimized single-level policies), and the dual decomposition suggests a computational path: solve pointwise problems parameterized by one multiplier per service level. If you’re building risk-averse decision layers on top of ML predictions, this gives a principled way to avoid “we tuned for p95 and broke p99.”

Davier et al. bring reliability thinking to multi-category scoring: a Potts/Ising-style rater agreement model where category-to-category “closeness” is weighted using LLM/SBERT embedding similarities. The practical payoff is you stop pretending category spacing is uniform or strictly ordinal—you model agreement directly, and “off by one category” can be treated as less severe (and empirically, it often is). Their near-agreement numbers are the eye-opener: exact accuracy can be mediocre while ±1-category agreement is high, which is often what operational stakeholders actually care about.

What to ponder this week

If we accept the premise that decision-quality is the objective, are we still comfortable running experiments optimized for parameter precision by default? Or should “regret / QoI risk / multi-level reliability” become the standard design target—especially now that surrogates and risk-aware objectives make it computationally feasible?

Featured Papers This Week

  • Mäkelburg et al.: Estimating Inconsistency Response Surfaces under Uncertainty in Cyber-Physical System Development (Experimental Design)
  • Higbee et al.: Experimental Design for Policy Choice (Experimental Design)
  • Farzaneh et al.: Risk-Averse Decision Making with Multi-Level Reliability Guarantees (Reliability)
  • Davier et al.: The Rater Ising-Potts Model with LLM-Derived Weights: An Application to Multi-Category Scoring Reliability (Reliability)
  • Jakeman et al.: Risk-Aware Goal-Oriented Bayesian Optimal Experimental Design (Experimental Design)
